speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, March 8, consideration of the motion of Hon. Mr. Rhodes for the second reading of Bill No. 19, to incorporate the Bank of Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
"Are we in danger of
Fascism in Canada?" is a question sometimes asked among the workers. Thinking in terms of brown shirts, parades and salutes I would say no, but when I come to a measure of this kind I am rather doubtful. In the days of the Romans we are told it was their practice to erect two upright spears, then place one transversely upon them and force their conquered enemies to pass under the spears, sub jugum-under the yoke-and usually a heavy tribute was exacted from the conquered enemies. It would seem to me that in the bill now before us we are arranging for the people of Canada to pass under the yoke, and if the bill is passed they must expect to pay a heavy tribute in the years to come.
For years we have had in this country a financial dictatorship but it has been somewhat concealed. By this legislation, instead of challenging that dictatorship, we are in reality legalizing and stabilizing it. The Finance minister warns us against any possible delay in giving the people the benefits of a central bank. I would say that the people have waited for some years for a central bank, and I think they can afford to wait a little longer rather than that we should saddle this country with what I regard as a private tyranny.
The bill provides for the creation of a private central bank. The amendment which we moved from this corner would seek to alter that so as to make the bank a public bank, but that amendment has been ruled out of order. Under those circumstances I think I must join with my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland) and take the position that the only course for us is to vote against

Bank of Canada-Mr. Woodsworth
this bill. I cannot see how we can possibly separate the bill from its contents. The main principle of the bill is that the bank shall be a privately owned institution. That is the proposal which comes before us. Could we have altered that to a publicy owned bank I would gladly have voted for the bill.
Let me point out that we do not object to a commission or board with wide powers, but we do object to the setting up of a body independent of and superior to the authority of parliament. I must quote again the statement of the Finance minister in reply to a question by my colleague from Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) because I do not think it can be broadcast too widely. He asked:
Supposing the central bank was endeavouring to regulate the control of credit in Canada, and supposing the policy it adopted in order to do so was contrary to the policy of the government of the day and they clashed, which official would make the decision?
The answer of the Finance minister was: Unquestionably the authority of the governor and the board of directors of the bank would prevail.
Here we have the unequivocal statement that we are at the moment being asked to erect a body whose decision would be superior to that of the government, It is an abdication of the powers of parliament. The Finance minister in order to try to justify his position is driven to the most specious reasoning. He refers to the board of railway commissioners. I submit that there is no such sovereign power given to the board of railway commissioners. It is true that they are free from everyday interference in the carrying on of their work, as undoubtedly this bank should be,, but still the great railway policies of this country are decided, not by the board of railway commissioners, but by this parliament. I recall that a few years ago, even with regard to a specific matter, that of the Crowsnest pass agreement, this parliament overrode the decision of the railway commission, and last year the special railway legislation which was passed surely indicated the supreme power of this parliament.
The Finance minister also referred to the tariff board, but again I point out that there is no sovereign authority in the tariff board. The tariff board does not override the decisions of this house. It may perform a valuable function, but still its reports go to the government. The government assumes responsibility, and we ratify or reject the measures that are in consequence brought down.

Because the Finance minister said that if there was a clash the will of the bank should prevail.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
With the government,
not with parliament.

There may be a
distinction there, but I doubt it very much. But I am glad that the Prime Minister is now being converted to the idea that parliament, rather than the government, should be supreme. It is a new doctrine from him, very new, for all along he has taken the ground that it was the government that assumed supreme responsibility, and we know that only in the most indirect fashion indeed has this government thought that it had to come to parliament. I think that that reasoning does not carry us very far.
The Finance minister also refers to the civil service commission, and suggests that it too is free from interference. Well, if I may venture on a colloquialism, it is to laugh, for anyone who knows the pressure that has been exerted from day to day on the civil service commission and the large number of reservations that are constantly being made of positions that are not to be filled by the commission will understand how little real independence has been exercised either under this government or the governmnt that preceded it, by the civil service commission. If the bank was to be as subject to as much interference as the civil service commission the situation would indeed be a difficult one. No one would suggest that it be subjected to interference as is the civil service commission. At the same time I say that it would be an impossible situation if the authority of the governor of the bank were to be superior to that of the government of this country.
It is true that the powers of parliament are being curtailed. The decisions of the Imperial conference have the effect of practically taking over taxing powers. Again, in connection with our estimates we have large blocks of
Bank of Canada-Mr. COMMONS
Woodsworth
expenditures which we commonly call uncontrollable expenditures. A recent bulletin of the Citizen's Research Institute states:
Including the interest paid by the dominion on guaranteed railway bonds, the total debt service cost $193,894,024, or $3,700,000 per week. This item alone cost $18.45 per capita, or 63 per cent of the gross revenue.
That is, 63 per cent of our gross revenue under present conditions does not come within the control of this parliament but automatically goes to the debt service.
By this bill we place under private ownership and control the issuance of currency, always regarded as the prerogative of the crown, and secondly the control of price levels, which is most important to the whole financial and economic life of this country. I should like to ask where is the leader of His Majesty's opposition at this time. He likes to boast that his grandfather helped to secure responsible government in Canada, but now it would seem that he himself acquiesces in the great betrayal, for such I think it will be considered in the years to come. We are taking away truly responsible government in this country in one of the most important spheres in which government should have control.

The right hon. gentleman
has not yet decided whether to do one thing or the other.

While the discussion was going on last night there lay on my table the evening newspaper in which appeared a fine photograph of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) arm in arm. It is delightful to know that they do find it possible to avoid political differences.
If the hon. member were there, would he have refused to be photographed?

It is very delightful to see these two gentlemen together and it would seem to be someiwhat symbolical. In dealing with this bill1 we are now finding that in the realm of financial affairs as well as in connection with a centennial celebration these two gentlemen can walk hand in hand,

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: While the lamp holds out to burn, the vilest sinner may return.
Who is the sinner?
What year was that?

In 1924; and that is precisely what happened to himself and his own government. Apparently, with his eyes wide open to the exact situation, he allowed himself to be duped a few years later and the bankers again won. Now we are proposing in this legislation to set up a domination of bankers or of a banker who will be able to defy the government that is in power. That is the actual situation. Further behind that banker would be the international bankers.
I agree with the minister that a central bank is a natural and inevitable development of our financial system. The chartered banks are essentially commercial banks, but their
1328	COMMONS
Bank oj Canada-Mr. Woodsworth
functions have been gradually extended until they have not only become deposit banks, taking in the savings of the people and on the basis of this providing for short term loans-and I may point out that they have gone on the basis of a ratio of ten to one- but in addition to that, through the provisions of the Bank Act and because of the lack of adequate machinery to put into operation the provisions of the Finance Act, these commercial banks have in practice been banka of issue. They have influenced price levels and, further, they have exercised an influence on foreign exchange matters and have been the government's own bankers. One might have thought that was sufficiently wide scope, but in more recent years they have entered the field of investment banking, either directly, taking up certain issues, or more generally indirectly through the means of the interlocking directorates of which we heard the other day. In addition to that they have been expected to supply agricultural credit.	This has been done through the
extension of short term credits by arrangements that have proved ruinous to the farmers and have left them without the power of securing further loans, even short term loans, from the banks.
This central bank legislation proposes to take over at least four of these functions I have enumerated. The central bank is to become a bank of issue. Its obligation will be to control price levels, and it will arrange foreign exchange matters and act as the government's bank. This, I suppose, is not the place to discuss the need for control over the distribution of credit; but that would still be quite untouched by the proposed central bank. I would point out that banking is the key industry which affects all others; no industry can be carried on without adequate supplies of credit. Banks alone, under modern conditions, are able to supply these credits, and they cannot only make credit in general cheap or dear, scarce or abundant, but they can also direct credit to one industry or firm rather than to another, and so prevent industrial expansion in this or that field. In our judgment, credit is of the nature of a public utility and should he publicly controlled.
This is not the place either for me to discuss the need for adequate agricultural credit, but I would point out in passing that this should enter into any general scheme of Canadian financial reorganization.
Again this is not the place I suppose to discuss the need for a national investment board, but I would point out that neither the proposed revision of the Bank Act nor
TMr. Woodsworth.]
this bill which we have under consideration to-day provides for such a board. If the principle of the nationalization of insurance, which was advanced from this corner the other day, could be adopted, we should have abundant funds available for investment purposes. To-day these funds are all gathered up and put in the hands of private institutions for investment. If national insurance were carried into effect all these funds would be gathered up and made available for an investment board to put into such enterprises as were socially of value.
So far as I can see, the main objection to a publicly-owned bank seems to be that it would be subject to political pressure if indeed it would not leave the way open for political corruption. It does seem to me that if we adopt that attitude the statement of my hon. friend from Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) becomes true and we simply recognize that parliament to-day has ceased to be of value to the people. The argument goes altogether too far. If we are not able to govern in the sphere of finance we are not able to govern in lesser spheres, and if we do not gov-rn finance, then it is only a question of time until government in other spheres becomes a veritable farce. I should rather like to think that by means of added responsibility we should gradually come to a higher conception of government. As J. A. Hobson said some time ago:
May not the conception of public control as a junto of officials and politicians, slowly grinding their own axes, be displaced by a more intelligent conception of a really representative control in which the various factors comprising the public interest shall be duly represented under a system removed from immediate political or class pressures?
If there are objections on the ground of possible dangers under a publicly-owned bank, it seems to me that there are also decided objections to, and inevitable dangers [DOT],n a privately-owned institution. Undoubtedly class interests would prevail; only fairly well to do people could own stock; and, as was pointed out last night by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland), this means, as in ordinary companies, that the control would not be widespread but would rather be concentrated in a few hands, ultimately in the hands probably of one person. This was very well expressed in a short paragraph I was reading the other day in a book by John Strachey:
It. is quite true that claims to a participation in the profits of the great modern centralized and concentrated enterprises are now, by means of the sale of shares, quite widely distributed amongst members of the property-

Bank of Canada-Mr. Woodsworth
owning class. But it is very naive to suppose that this constitutes any diffusion of effective ownership or control. A small shareholder, or indeed the whole body of small shareholders collectively, in a great modern company, have about as much control over it as they have over the Grand llama of Tibet. They take what dividends the directors, who own the controlling blocks of shares, like to pay them, and read, devoutly, the financial columns of their newspapers, where city editors tell them what the big capitalists want them to think.
That is about what would happen in the case of a national bank if it were organized on the basis proposed in this bill.
While I cannot go quite so far as my colleague the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) that the main cause of poverty in the midst of plenty is the money question, undoubtedly that question is of prime importance. May I ask: Can we look to such a bank as that which it is proposed to set up, to make any radical changes in the money system? I hold in my hands an article by Mr. A. de V. Leigh entitled Realities and Make-Belief published on March 25, 1933, in the Times Trade and Engineering Supplement from which I quote the following:
The experts .are like squirrels, able to crack nuts-however hard these may be-with the greatest skill and cleverness, but being, so far as progression is concerned, circumscribed by their cages, they can only run round and round in circles. They recognize that what is necessary is to put more tokens into the pockets of consumers, but these tokens can be obtained only by being borrowed at interest. This implies repayment of more than has been put in, so that they are once more back at the point of only being able to recommend more debt to cure a system which is breaking down on account of too much debt.
I would point out that if it becomes necessary to change the money system, it is extremely difficult to have this done by a bank that is to a large extent removed from the pressure of public opinion and that also by its very constitution is in the hands of those who are interested not only in maintaining the status quo but also in seeing that their own immediate financial investments are protected. The bank must make money and one cannot read the reports of the Bank of England without realizing that that bank is not altogether indifferent to the dividends paid to its shareholders. Further, suppose by any chance the time might come in this country when the people generally think, in order to relieve themselves of the burden of debt, some sort of reflationary process is necessary. Would a privately owned bank agree to anything of this kind? I cannot think that is possible. A privately owned bank is in the hands of people who would undoubtedly lose money by such a process.
Some years ago France got rid of the greater part of her public debt by a process commonly called inflation when the franc was reduced from 20 cents to 4 cents. I wonder whether that would be possible if we had a privately owned bank in this country, in which not only the stock was owned by private individuals but the management was under the control of a governor not responsible to the dominion government. Again may I read a paragraph from a very interesting book called What Everybody Wants to Know About Money, edited by G. D. H. Cole. I think he puts the whole situation very clearly:
More than once it has become plain that the only real alternative to government control of the banking system has been, not the separation of the financial and political powers, but rather the control of the political by the financial authority. The British Labour government of 1931 is by no means the only government that has been brought down since the war by the action of the financial world. For example, the same fate overtook the short-lived socialist government of Norway, and bankers' pressure upon governments has been a familiar feature of the world's history during the past dozen years. It is no easier for banks and governments to separate their spheres of jurisdiction to-day than it was in medieval Europe for pope and emperor to live side by side without clash-ings of authority.
In these circumstances the question appears nowadays to many people to be not whether bankers ought to be allowed to carry on their own business without public interference, but whether governments or banks are to have the last word in matters in which they are both inevitably concerned.
That is a clear statement of the issue before us to-day. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) has stated very distinctly that when there is a clash, the bankers are to have the last word. We in this comer-and' I hope we shall be joined by at least some members of the Liberal party-would like to provide that when there is a clash, the government must have the last word because in the long run the government is responsible to the people. Such a bank would be quite removed from contact with the ordinary rank and file of the people; its governor would not be required to present himself for election nor to keep in touch with nor to be guided by the will of the people. If we have reached that stage, it is about time we give up even the semblance of democracy. Surely the people themselves have the right to decide. Whilst we talk about the danger of political influence, we must remember that if we have no political influence we are thereby giving up the very essence, the very foundation of democracy. It may very well be that sometimes democracy may make mistakes in its decisions, but that is the only way in which
1330	COMMONS
Bank of Canada-Mr. Spencer
higher levels can be attained. We believe the ultimate control of policy should rest with government, but detailed administration should be left to the appointed board; that governments should have the right to appoint and dismiss members of the board; that there should be a minister of state responsible for answering in parliament for the affairs of the board, but that parliamentary discussions of financial matters should be confined to questions of policy and not matters of detail.
We find a very fine example of this in the arrangements connected with the British Broadcasting Corporation which is a separate corporation, if you like, but the control of which finally is with the government. There is to a certain extent a similar arrangement in Great Britain under the Central Electricity Board. I cannot see why some such arrangement cannot be adopted in this country whereby we may have a board having under its control this bank and directing its administration but in its general policies subject to the government and to parliament.

Bank oj Canada-Mr. Spencer
was no less a man than Sir Charles Addis who at one time was connected, if not now, with the Bank of International Settlements; when we recognize, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) that two officials of the Bank of England travelled across Canada with the commission, the presence of whom was not advertised, are we to take it for granted that there was some pressure exerted in connection with the setting up of a central bank which would have the effect of bringing it under the influence of the Bank of England? While on the one hand I must congratulate the government of the day upon doing all they can to guard against private bank control of the central bank, on the other hand, there seems to be a real danger, and one which I believe we have overlooked, of a possible disadvantageous influence from outside banks such as the Bank of England or the Bank of International Settlements over the Bank of Canada. There does not seem to be a realization of the influence such a condition may have upon the whole country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? In view of what he has said, how does he justify his action last year in voting to tie the dollar to the pound sterling?

That is not entirely in line with the argument I am placing before [DOT] hon. members at the present time. At particular times it may be worth while to tie the dollar to the pound sterling. But what I am trying to emphasize is this, that Canada should be mistress of her own house. The market to which wm should pay most attention is the market within Canada. Our first aim should be to see that our people, with their great possibilities for production of goods and services, should be able to take full advantage of them. Our people can take full advantage of those possibilities if we have a financial system which at all times will enable them to have sufficient purchasing power, so that they may be enabled to make those exchanges. And if, as has been done in the past, we find ourselves in the position where on the one hand we have an abundance of goods and sendees while on the other we have an increasing number of people who are not only unemployed but under employed, and therefore not in a position to make those purchases, or in a position to take the fullest advantage of our great powers of production and services, we invite inevitable chaos. The fear I have therefore, is of adverse effects upon our whole financial system brought about by outside influence.

Last night the hon. member for Bow River placed on record some figures with respect to the total assets and liabilities of Canadian banks. He took the liabilities from the assets and showed in each case the balance in favour of the banks. Then he went on to show how much of what is now known as the C.P.R. loan of $60,000,000, was taken up by each of those banks. Without taking up the time of the house by repeating the figures I should like to make some observations in this connection. One big bank in Canada which had an excess of assets over liabilities of $1,551,159 took a share of the C.P.R. loan equal to $22,404,000. Another one with a balance of assets over liabilities amounting to $699,612 made a loan of $5,180,000. A third one with assets over liabilities amounting to $1,818,499 made a loan of $12,280,000. One may wonder how this was done, but the explanation is very simple. The situation shows, first of all, that the banks did not loan other people's deposits, because in each of these cases they loaned from six to ten times the total amount of the balance between their assets and their liabilities. As the Prime Minister quite properly pointed out, it shows that the security was put up by the company in question, backed, by the way, by the guarantee of the dominion government. What was it that enabled the banks to write into existence this $60,000,000? It was the security put up by the railway company, in the first instance, supported by the guarantee of the federal government. Therefore the transaction is based entirely .on the assets and on the credit first of the railway company and secondly on the credit of the nation. It is because the banking fraternity have taken the privilege, and have been allowed to write credits into existence to any amount that they could get away with, and because such action is permitted, that we take the stand, that such an important function should be under much more drastic government control. When we face the possibility of having a government bank, a Bank of Canada, we feel that such an institution should be entirely under governmental control and not in private hands. Although there have been certain safeguards allowed-and we sincerely hope those safeguards will prove effective-at the same time there is no guarantee that they will be effective. We in this section of the house fear that the safeguards will not be strong enough, and that ultimately the institution will come under complete private control.
The present Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) one of the ablest members in this house, and as we know, an authority on financial matters,

Bank oj Canada-Mr. Spencer
when speaking in Toronto last year made two outstanding statements. The first was:
Bank deposits consist largely of credit money which has been created by the banks.
I have just outlined that that was done with regard to the Canadian Pacific loan. The second statement was:
The cheque system enables the banks to create credit money at will.
Of course, that is along similar lines. It is clear that, first, the creation and control of credit money is part of the crown's prerogative. Secondly, that prerogative is created for the benefit of the people and cannot be exercised to their prejudice. Thirdly, that prerogative has not been parted with, and cannot be parted with except by statute. Fourthly, the exercise of this power by any private corporation is without 'legal warrant, and consequently is illegal, differing in degree only and not in kind from the art of the counterfeiter. Fifthly, it is not in the interest of the state to renounce its sovereignty. It is because of these considerations that we lay so much stTess upon parliament not giving up its control of the creation of credit and of money matters in general because through the control of private interests whose main incentive is profit, and who favour certain businesses with which the banks are connected by interlocking directorates, these great functions have not been always and may not be exercised in the interests of the state.
Our real problem, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me is one of purchasing power. In purchasing power can be found the key to various problems that we have confronting us at this time. It is the key, for instance, to the unemployment problem. It is the key to the underemployment problem. It is the key to the undernourishment problem, because we know full well that if this country with its vast riches of goods and everything that is required in the matter of food, clothing and shelter made proper use of its powers of production, plus its powers of distribution, there need not be anyone undernourished. Again, it is the key to the glut of commodities, because if we had proper means of transferring the many commodities that we make to the people who want them there should be no glut. Any surplus there might be would 'be very small indeed. Purchasing power is the key also to the stagnation of our trade. Some .people think that trading must be done first before you can obtain money, but you must have money in some form before you can trade. If those who control money simply decided to take it out
of existence by cancellation of loans, which can be done so easily under our financial system, it would at once put a crimp intc our trade and would make trading impossible except by way of barter.
Lastly, the lack of purchasing power is in no small degree responsible for our difficulties with regard to taxation. A large proportion of our people are not in a position to pay their taxes. Further, when I remind this house that the total amount of income tax that is paid annually in this country is paid by less than three per cent of the population, in other words that 97 per cent of our people have not a sufficient income upon which to pay income tax, I think it will be recognized by everybody that something is wrong with our financial system.
In closing, I should like to put on record the reasons for the lag in purchasing power. I quote from the New English Weekly, a well known English paper:
So much misunderstanding, misrepresentation and misinterpretation has lately overlaid the discussion whether industry distributes a deficiency of purchasing that it is necessary for us categorically to restate the causes of the obvious deficiency. The passage from Major Douglas' "The New and the Old Economics," and our columns are open to any Goliath of economics to show us where we are wrong.
Categorically there are at least the following five causes of a deficiency of purchasing power as compared with the collective prices of goods on sale:
(11 Money profits collected from the public (interest is profit on an intangible).
(2)	Savings, i.e. mere abstention from buying.
Everyone must recognize that to the extent that savings are not used to buy goods or services or loaned to others to buy goods there must be an equivalent amount of goods and services idle. It goes on:
(3)	Investment of savings in new works which create a new coat without fresh purchasing power.
(4)	Difference in circuit velocity between cost liquidation and price creation, which results in charges being carried over into prices from a previous cost-accounting cycle. Practically all plant charges are of this nature, and all payments for material brought in from a previous wage-cycle are of the same nature.
(5)	Deflation, i.e. sale of securities by banks and recall of loans.
With regard to the last-mentioned cause of the lag in purchasing power, we are giving to the central bank known as the Bank of Canada the power of inflation and deflation within proper limits, also the sale and purchase of securities, the making of loans to the federal and provincial governments and to banks, and the recalling of those loans. If the strings which the government are providing in this

Bank of Canada-Mr. Lucas
act in order to make the bank function as a semi-government bank are sound and strong, well and good; but we are afraid that they may not be strong enough to take care of the interests of the public. It is for that reason that we criticize severely the setting up of this Bank of Canada and turning it over to the control of private shareholders, who, through the manipulation of share control in the years to come, may bring the bank under the control of a few people, just as we find the shares of our private banks to-day in the hands of a few. If that takes place, not only shall we have lost one of the greatest opportunities that we have ever had of placing this country in a position to start out on a new era of prosperity, with a new and better standard of living, but we shall find ourselves in an infinitely worse position than we are in to-day.

Mr. Speaker, in introducing the resolution on which the present bill is founded, the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) made the following statement, which will be found at page 824 of Hansard:
The bill which is founded upon this resolution is one of unusual importance and significance.
That is a statement upon which I think all parties in the house are agreed. The Finance minister went on to say:
It marks an advanced stage in our economic and financial development as a nation. The proposed central bank should not, I submit, be regarded as a break with the past; we are not departing from the system which was served us so well. Rather the central bank should be regarded as another stage in the natural evolution of our banking system.
I feel sure, Mr. Speaker, that that is tantamount to saying to the Canadian people that the evolution will be so gradual that they need not expect to see any change come from the establishment of this central bank. I was sorry to hear the minister make the statement that we should not expect any break with the past. I believe when the great war ended there was a distinct cleavage with the past. As the soldier was demobilized and fumigated, he left off his old uniform, put on a new suit of clothes and went out to face a new world. While it may have taken ten or eleven years to recognize this fact, I think that what occurred during the great collapse of 1929 and the four years of depression which followed has brought home to us the realization that we must face the future with an entirely new outlook and that we can never go back to pre-war day conditions. The minister stated that this proposed legislation marked an advanced stage in the economic and financial

development of the nation. We have been told that thirty-six nations already have central banks, most of them privately owned. Will any hon. member say that any of those nations with privately owned central banks were outstanding in preventing unemployment or easing the situation through the great depression? It seems to me that we are simply placing ourselves in the same position as those nations which accepted central banks some years ago, and therefore adding to the danger of a world domination of banking policy.
Realizing the importance of this question, earlier in the session I introduced a resolution asking for a national system of credit and finance to be controlled in the interests of all the people. My object in doing so was to bring on a discussion of this very important question before any banking legislation was brought down. I sought to have the government fully advised of the views of the members of the house before committing themselves to any definite legislation. I was told that as my resolution anticipated legislation to be brought down, the time was not opportune for the carrying on of such a discussion. We now find that both the old parties feel that the second reading of the bill is not the proper time to discuss this question. Not long ago an eminent professor in the United States stated that there were only sixteen men in the world who understood anything about finance. There was no Canadian in that list, but I ask hon. members not to take the professor too seriously. During the debate on my resolution the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) seemed to take the opinion of this professor as final and to assume that the question of finance was too vast and sacred to be discussed by the ordinary individual. In fact, the minister went so far as to twit myself and the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) with having the temerity to rush in where angels feared to tread. I do not lay any claim to being a financial expert, but I think I can say without any spirit of egotism that I possess, at least I hope I do, average intelligence and common sense; and I believe if these qualities alone were applied, some solution of our difficulties might be found.
In claiming that our present financial system is at fault I find myself in very good company. One has only to quote the inaugural address of President Roosevelt made last year and recall his indictment of the system and the money changers. One could quote scores of other prominent people

Bank of Canada-Mr. Lucas
throughout the world who are convinced that the root of our trouble lies in our financial system. I should like to put on record a statement of a former governor of the Bank of England, Mr. Vincent Vickers, who said in 1932:
Obviously he (the Chancellor of the Exchequer) must rely upon the long experience and the wider knowledge of the Bank of England; but when things go wrong, terribly wrong; when we are told one day that the national safety depends upon the adherence to the gold standard no matter what the sacrifice; and a week or so later that our abandonment of it will bring salvation and prosperity to our industries; when the pulling of old levers no longer moves the signals; when the patient no longer responds to the old prescriptions . . . then surely it is time for the government to seek advice elsewhere, and to encourage open discussion, rather than attempt to "shelve" the question, as was done at Ottawa, and to avoid the issue because it is so difficult.
The fear of discussing monetary questions is a splendid example of the atmosphere which has been built up around the whole matter of finance. We have been taught to believe that finance was a subject for supermen and that it was the rankest kind of heresy and sacrilege for an ordinary individual to delve into the matter. It was surrounded more or less with a veil of mystery. But the disclosures of the last few years have rent that veil asunder and the picture disclosed was not altogether a pleasant one. With the idea prevailing that finance was a subject for supermen, the result has been that the ordinary individual has given very little thought to it. To-day we find that Mr. Average Citizen knows very little about financial matters. However, that condition is changing rapidly and to-day throughout western Canada many study clubs are engaged in the discussion of monetary problems. Right in this city there are many such clubs and one has only to travel across Canada in a smoking compartment to realize that finance is the main topic of discussion among the people. Speaking on the British budget in April, 1932, Sir Robert Horne said:
These questions of currency always seem very remote from the ordinary life of the people, who have not had to consider them for more than 100 years, and yet the question of currency sits down at every table that is spread with a meal in every cottage or castle throughout the country.
Aristotle said that money exists not by nature but by law; it is the law that says what shall be legal tender, and it is in this house that we make the laws. I think everyone admits that there is something wrong, but when we come to decide just what it is there seem to be almost as many opinions as there
are people. In my opinion, it is important that we first make a proper diagnosis of our trouble. When this is done we may then be in a better position to deal with it. In this house there are many hon. gentlemen who are prominent in the medical profession, and I think they will agree with me that the most important thing a medical man has to do when called to see a patient is first to make a proper diagnosis of the disease. As a matter of fact, until that is done more harm than good may come to the patient. If the doctor cannot tell at a glance what is wrong with the patient, I understand that he begins what is known as the process of elimination. In other words, he will first test the heart and if he finds it functioning properly he eliminates that organ for the time being, then examines the lungs, the liver and so on, eliminating each organ as he finds it properly performing its function. Now, if we apply that test to our body politic we can start with agriculture, and I presume that if I asked whether there was anything wrong with agriculture to-day almost everyone in the country would hold up both hands. But let me ask, what is the function of agriculture? The answer is the function of agriculture is to produce the foodstuffs required by the people of the world; and will anyone say that agriculture is failing in that respect? I do not think anyone will say so when we find the elevators bursting with grain, and that a policy of curtailment of production is proposed. Indeed, we see various countries destroying a part of their crops; we learn of coffee being burned, of cotton being ploughed under. I doubt whether there is a country in the world where the farmers are producing as much per capita as they are right in the Dominion of Canada. So far as agriculture is concerned therefore I think we can very well eliminate it in our search for the trouble; it is performing its function one hundred per cent.
Let us turn then to industry; and when we find many of the great factories in the last few years have either closed down or have been running part time, unable to sell their goods, their one great desire being to open up and to manufacture the things people need. We must admit, therefore, that so far as industry is concerned, it was never more efficient, never more prepared to supply the needs of people everywhere. And so we eliminate industry.
What about transportation? Was there ever a time in the history of the world when all the means of transportation were so efficient,



Bank of Canada-Mr. Lucas
never were we able to transport goods to the far corners of the earth so rapidly. And so we eliminate transportation.
Coming to labour, I would ask whether labour was ever more efficient than it is at the present time. Is labour refusing to work?
I say, no. When we find thousands of people unemployed, not because they wish to be idle but 'because they cannot get an opportunity to earn a decent living, we must conclude that there is unemployment for some particular reason. One has only to read the evidence that has been adduced in the committee on mass buying and spreads to see where labourers have been working from fifty, sixty, to seventy-five hours a week and receiving only from $1.60 to $6.50 a week. I claim that when any individual works such long hours for such a pittance, it is evidence that labour is doing its utmost to earn a living and so keep away from charity. We have to confess therefore that labour is performing its function efficiently.
This brings us to the next organism that functions in the body politic, namely, finance. Now, what is the function of finance? In my opinion its proper function is to facilitate the exchange of goods. It is the link between production and consumption, and here we find every one of the organisms that go to make u,p the body politic anxious to perform its particular function and, indeed, performing it on the physical side 100 per cent, and yet because of the financial system the people are not able to make use of the goods which we are in a position to produce. It is the burden of debt which is strangling these various organisms and like a cancer will finally destroy them.
Let me give an illustration. A customer wants a box of matches; the storekeeper has matches on the shelf: what is the thing that keeps them apart? If the man has money in his pocket and walks in and lays the money on the counter he can walk out with the matches, but if he has no money no transaction takes place. Money is the link which connects the two. The thing we have to realize is that we have passed from the age of our ancestors, which was an age of real scarcity. The present money system was developed under that condition and apparently it will not function in an age of plenty. Our only scarcity to-day is artificial. I believe I am right in saying that there is practically no demand for goods that cannot be met if we are able to place the money on the table: yet there is a vast unfilled demand. On one side we find producers straining to produce, while on the other side there is un-

employment, with consumers not allowed to consume. Something stands between, and that thing is finance.
I might give another illustration. Here is a beautiful section of country divided by a very deep ravine. People wish to trade with one another and they decide to build a bridge. That bridge is built, not simply as a thing of beauty to look at but for service. By and by trade develops and the bridge is no longer large enough to accommodate the traffic between the two sections of the country and so the people decide that they will have either to enlarge the bridge or to build a new one to take care of the increased traffic. They do not say, "The bridge not being large enough, we will restrict the traffic to suit the bridge." But apparently that is what we are doing today in the matter of finance. We are capable of producing in vast quantities, but because we. cannot get sufficient tickets or tokens for the exchange of goods we are starting on a policy of curtailment, trying to limit the wants of people to the amount of money the banks see fit to let them have.
Professor Murdock of Perth university, in the New Era of Sydney, Australia, has written an article which admirably describes the situation:
The world is not suffering from a lack of goods to-day, but from a lack of tickets for the exchange of goods. To give you a picture of what is happening in this world of ours, I must ask you to imagine a village-not a poor village-but a very wealthy one-threatened with floods. All the villagers come in haste to the railway station, where as it happens there is a train large enough to accommodate all of them, with steam up ready to go. They rush on board, but the guard comes along and asks them to show their tickets. Rather impatient, because the waters are rising rapidly, they get out and rush to the ticket office, only to be'told that unfortunately there are no tickets to be had; the last were sold yesterday, and no new supplies have come along. They all rush back to the train, where they find the engine-driver engaged in putting out his fires. "I'm very sorrj%" says the station-master, "but I'm afraid you'll have to drown. If it's any consolation to you to know it, I shall have to drown with you. There's no help for it. Obviously the train can't carry passengers who haven't got tickets. That has never yet been allowed." So they all drown for lack of tickets.
What would you think of a railway company which, instead of printing tickets sufficient for the number of passengers it might be required to carry, limited the number of passengers and the number of trains to make them fit the number of tickets it had' printed? That is what happens in the world to-day.
Instead of creating the right amount of money to carry on all the business possible in the world, rve limit the business to make it fit the amount of money there is. We close factories, we limit production, we throw men

out of work, we starve people, simply and solely for lack of money; and yet money is a thing we can create in precisely whatever quantities we choose.
May I ask the hon. gentleman who wrote that article?

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Smith (Cumberland) in the chair.
Miscellaneous services relating to navigation and shipping, $35,000.

What is the reason for this
decrease ?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: There is a saving in the spending of this item.

What is the $35,000 spent
for?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The proposed appropriation includes necessary provision for the examination of masters and mates, $14,300; navigation schools, $5,700; temporary relief for distressed seamen, $2,500; investigation into wrecks, $5,000; registration of shipping, $2,000; removal of obstructions in navigable waters, $1,500 and inspection of livestock shipments, $4,000. In the year 1932-33 the expenditure was $28,605. I must add that the expenditure up to the present date in this fiscal year is $25,000. For that reason we believe $35,000 will be a sufficient vote.
Where are navigation schools established in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
There is a school at
Halifax, and also schools at Yarmouth, Saint John, NjB., Quebec and Prince Rupert. There is also a grant to the navigation school at Queens university.
Does the minister think there are sufficient schools of navigation to encourage young men to take to the sea?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: These schools are not instituted for the purpose of inviting young men to go into navigation, or to take training in navigation. The purpose of the schools is to offer them an opportunity to study navigation so that they may obtain their certificates as mates, seamen and masters.

I understand that, but it
seems to me that if there were sufficient
Supply-M arine

schools in the country more young men would be likely to apply for masters' and mates' certificates. The difficulty now is that these schools are so placed that it is a hardship for many of the young men in Nova Scotia to attend; they have difficulty in getting to Halifax or to Yarmouth. My idea is that in a number of Nova Scotian ports, where there is shipping, other schools could be established at small cost.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: If we may judge by the attendance of young men at these schools I do not think it could be said that more schools are needed. For instance, the Halifax school is open during twelve months of the year, but the average monthly attendance is only seven. That school serves the whole province.

I am afraid the argument
used by the minister is not a good one. I have always been taught that most of the brilliant young Canadians come from the farm or the village. Take Scotchmen, if you wish- I know of thousands of young men born in the highlands of Scotland away from the cities and towns who, like Dick Whittingdon, travelled to London and took charge of the government of Great Britain. I know, further, of a number of cases in this great Dominion of Canada where men born on farms or in little fishing villages on the Atlantic or Pacific coasts, have gone far in the life of this country. I do not expect that many people in the city of Halifax will attend the navigation school; no one would expect they would. That is the reason I have hinted to the minister that it would be much better to close the navigation school at Halifax and to open small schools in other parts of the province within easy reach of the seamen. It is a hardship for the people from Cape North or Neil's Harbour, or Canso, to go to Halifax to attend school for three or four months so as to obtain the necessary knowledge to become a mate. The same statements would apply to the western part of the province. For instance, let us consider the county in which I live. My opinion is that there should be a school for seamen and sailors in the county of Lunenburg, because it is in that county sailors are made. They do not make them in Antigonish, but they make them in part of Guysborough. There should be a school at Canso; there might be another one at Sherbrooke. As I say, the fact that only seven students attend the navigation school at Halifax is not an argument against the establishment of further schools. I must say that the teacher at the Halifax school is a most estimable gentleman;

he knows his business, and it is not his fault that there are only seven pupils.
The point I am trying to impress upon the minister is this, however, that the department should endeavour to establish small schools in the rural sections of the province, and not particularly in the city of Halifax. The trouble in Nova Scotia is -that Halifax is getting too much. In my opinion it would be a good thing to put a fence around Halifax, and do something for the rest of the province.

The minister has said there is one school in the city of Quebec. What opportunity does that offer the people of Bonaventure and Gaspe who are living four hundred or five hundred miles away from Quebec? What advantage is the Quebec school to those poor fishermen who wish to enter schools of navigation?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I understand that
young men who wish to qualify as seamen obtain their early experience on steamships, or some other type of boat, and when they have acquired a certain degree of experience they attend schools and study for the purpose of obtaining -the certificate of a master or mate. I understand that those young men who are anxious to gain their livelihood in that line of work gladly go from Gaspe to Quebec for the purpose of studying for a few months. At that point they take their examinations.

Does the minister imagine that under the present state of affairs, with fish selling at about two cents per pound, young men from Gaspe and Bonaventure could afford to attend the school at Quebec? Would it not be better to open a school in the Gaspe peninsula which is four hundred or five hundred miles from Quebec, so that those young men could have an opportunity to qualify?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
May I remind the
hon. member that the men in charge of fishing vessels do not require masters' certificates.

But outside of men on fishing vessels, may I point out that there are fishermen in Gaspe and Bonaventure who are five hundred miles away from Quebec. How can those poor people undertake to go to Quebec to follow a course of education? Why not establish a school of this kind somewhere on the Gaspe coast or on the north shore of the St. Lawrence between Chicoutimi and Saguenay where the fishermen live and where the sailors are born?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
We would gladly do it to please my hon. friend and his electors, but

Supply-Marine
it is not very convenient to establish schools in every part of all the provinces. We have a school now in nearly every province, one at Halifax and another at Yarmouth for Nova Scotia, one at Saint John for New Brunswick, one in the city of Quebec, one at Kingston and another at Collingwood for Ontario, and another at Prince Rupert for British Columbia. So far as I am aware there have been no complaints from the public that there is an insufficient number of navigation schools. We are disposed to do anything that is reasonable to help the navigators, but in these times when we have had to reduce expenditures generally we did not think of increasing the number of schools. But in the future, if things continue to improve, as I think they are improving, if we see there is a necessity for more schools, this government will be disposed to do anything reasonable.
Mr. MARCH.: Can the minister say how many students attended the school at Quebec last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Last year the school at Quebec was open for three months and had an average monthly attendance of sixteen.

You have a school in
Yarmouth, and it is not as far for Nova Scotians to go to Halifax as the distance from Gaspe to Quebec. Why should not the same argument apply for Quebec province as for Nova Scotia? If you have a second school in Nova Scotia, why not a second school in the province of Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I should hope the results would be better from a second school established in the province of Quebec than from the second school in Nova Scotia because at the school at Yarmouth, which has been open twelve months on half time, the average monthly attendance was only two, which is not very encouraging.
Move that school to Gaspe.

The minister says he is willing to give all the facilities that are required as conditions improve. Why should not the government itself start to improve conditions by giving to the young people on the Gaspe coast the facilities for learning a calling? They are all sailors and fishermen, and they have certainly not the means to go such a long distance as to the school at Quebec. I know the minister cannot finally decide the question to-day but I would ask him to consider fully whether this is not an opportune time for him to establish a school
to enable these young people to learn a calling. They live on the Atlantic coast, and naturally are all fishermen. They would ask for nothing better than the opportunity to qualify for a calling if they could only be given the chance by the government. I think the minister should consider the question of having a school either in Bonaventure or Gaspe for these young people who live such a long distance away from Quebec. The question has often been mooted. These young people of Bonaventure have no other trade or occupation to go into whereas there are many trades and occupations open to the people of Quebec city. Down on the Gaspe coast the opportunities are limited to farming, lumbering and fishing, and the minister knows that so far as fishing is concerned the Gaspe coast is far behind what it should be. Representations have been made to him time and time again by men of both political parties, and by such an eminent personage as His Excellency the Bishop of Gaspe, who is now taking charge of this question in the interests of his people. He has called the minister's attention repeatedly, I am sure, to the handicaps under which this population labours and to the condition of the fishing industry itself. I think application has been made for the establishment of a biological station down there. I do not like to bring that question up on the Marine estimates, but perhaps I might be allowed to make a reference to it. I should like to know from the minister if anything has been done in regard to the requests made by Bishop Ross and the people generally on the Gaspe coast. The question was discussed no later than yesterday or the day before in the Quebec legislature, and it was contended there that if an agreement could be arrived at between the two governments it would be for the benefit of the population. I have no doubt that the minister is impressed with the importance of the matter and is willing to do what is possible. He will admit that conditions at the present time are not at all satisfactory and that something should be done if we want to help these people to carry on their calling. I am not asking for the establishment of schools above Quebec in that part of the province where there are no fishermen or sailors, but down in that part of the province where the sea is the natural calling of the population. I hope that the minister, who acts in the dual capacity of Minister of Marine and Acting Minister of Fisheries, will come forward and say that the government of which he is
Supply-M arine

a member will give these people some encouragement and say that he is in favour of a progressive policy. If there is a misunderstanding, as it were, between the government at Quebec and the government at Ottawa because the fisheries of the province are under the control of the Quebec government, it is unfortunate that the population has to suffer on that account. It is for that reason that I bring this matter up, in the hope that the minister will be able to give us some encouragement, and tell us that he has considered this question and intends doing something. If he will give us some assurance on that point I am sure that his announce-' ment will be received with great pleasure by the population generally of that peninsula.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I should like to remind my hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) that we are not at the present time discussing the estimates of the Fisheries department. We are discussing the estimates of the Marine department. However, I have no objection to saying a few words on the question raised by my hon. friend. As he well knows, the fisheries were transferred to the provincial authorities in 1923, I think it was, at the request of the authorities in Quebec. Since then the fisheries have been under their absolute control, but nevertheless we were asked last year by the authorities at Quebec to cooperate and help them in the administration of the fisheries of that province. I had conferences with the Minister of Fisheries of Quebec, one at Quebec and another at Ottawa, and I expressed my strong desire as Acting Minister of Fisheries to help the Quebec authorities in the way suggested by my hon. friend. It was suggested that a French school might be established in Gaspe for the fishermen and to train inspectors of fisheries-a French school, which would be of service to the French fishermen of the province and of New Brunswick and the Magdalen islands. The Quebec government was supposed to supply the building, and two or three French teachers would be supplied by my department. The matter will be discussed further with the provincial authorities. I understand that the Quebec government has sent to Europe two or three young men who had already some knowledge in fishery matters in order that they may perfect their studies abroad. These young men may become the teachers of that school.
I hope to be in a position before long to do something in cooperation with the Fisheries department at Quebec.

I wish to thank the minister for his announcement. I know he
iMr. Marcil.]
realizes the importance of this matter. It is all right to have English-speaking schools in the English-speaking districts, but in a population which is largely French it is only fair that the people should be taught in the language in which they are the most competent. I understand the university of Laval has offered the services of young men or even professors who would be qualified to take up this matter and start it along. It is unfortunate that the population should suffer through a lack of cooperation between the two governments. I do not blame either this or the provincial government and I am glad to know that the minister realizes the importance of doing something for these people.
The Magdalen islands, the Gaspe coast, the noirth and south shores of the St. Lawrence, Gloucester, Shippigan and other places along there are inhabited almost solely by fishermen and sailors. If a start could be made at Gaspe, the centre of the whole district, I am sure considerable improvement would be made. The minister would be entitled to a great deal of credit if he continued his cooperation with the Quebec government. I am glad to know that Mr. LaFerte, the Minister of Fisheries of Quebec, has met the minister in this respect. The Bishop of Gaspe has offered his most sincere cooperation, as has the university of Laval. A sincere desire is expressed throughout the whole district that this great part of our national domain in which is carried on one of the great industries of Canada should receive the attention it deserves. These people are poor, they are hard working, they have to face hard winters and are handicapped in many respects. During the last three or four years there has been a marked decline in the lumbering industry and many shanties and mills have been closed throwing thousands of men out of employment. The fishermen are forced to work hard to eke out a living of the barest kind and they are entitled to all the assistance the minister can give.
I hope the minister will continue his efforts to bring about a better understanding. The province of Quebec controls these fisheries but the dominion government expends a lot of money in the improvement of fishing conditions and the distribution of knowledge in connection therewith. This fact was pointed out only a few weeks ago in the legislative council of Quebec by the Honourable Mr. Kelly, who resides at New Carlisle and who is an authority on fishing matters. He pointed out many ways in which agreement could be brought about between the two governments with the cooperation of Bishop

Supply-Marine
Ross. The bishop exercises great influence in the district and he has the interests of the people at heart. Fishing will always remain one of the main occupations of these people and I think some effort should be made to bring this matter to a conclusion as soon as possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I have followed the discussions and the debates which have taken place in the legislative council and the house at Quebec and during my trip last summer down the St. Lawrence I visited the fishermen of Quebec and New Brunswick. I was impressed by his competency to deal with these matters and I told him that this government would cooperate with the provincial government on the lines I have already stated. We are still of the same disposition.

I should like to know if the minister has instructed his deputy to go to Quebec, I understand that the premier of Quebec has made the announcement that negotiations were under way and that Mr. Found had been instructed to come down there to learn the views of the Quebec government and see how cooperation could be brought about. Could the hon. minister inform me whether the instruction in those schools is gratuitous?

At Halifax?

Many vessels were sailed from this port and in fact, many were built there and sold throughout the world. A great mercantile marine was built up, but this situation has changed to such an extent that now there are only two pupils in the school. I shall be pleased to take the matter into consideration and get more information, and if something can be done to improve the situation it will be done.
As to the other question, the reason inspectors of ship tackle have not yet been appointed is that my department have drawn up certain regulations for the prevention of accidents in loading or unloading ships and these regulations have been forwarded to all the shipping interests, associations of stevedores and so forth on the Pacific and Atlantic coasts for their study and report. As soon as this is completed, we intend to appoint inspectors where they are required.

It is all very well to send out regulations, but unless there is some official who has proper authority from the government, I do not think any regulation would be carried out at least officially. I would urge the minister to have an officer appointed very soon because ship tackle inspection is absolutely necessary. One of the first occasions upon which I rose in the house was to support the hon. member for Richelieu (Mr. Cardin), the former Minister of Marine, when the same question was up. Let us consider for a moment the object of these schools. A young man has been going to sea for a couple of years; he has ambition and he goes to the marine school to get some tuition in navigation and passes for second mate. He then goes back to sea as a second mate and after he has spent two years at sea, he returns with a certificate of servitude of two years. He goes again to school and applies for a

ticket as fii'st mate. He passes the examination; he gets his ticket and again goes to sea. After two years further service he returns to one of these navigation schools where he studies for a master's certificate and if he is successful, he gets it. These young men cannot travel long distances; they cannot go to Halifax and spend five dollars a day for board and tuition, so these schools should be planted in at least three or four places in the maritime provinces. Forty years ago Yarmouth had more sail tonnage than any other port in Canada, but that has evaporated. Why? simply because steam drove sail off the ocean. In the seventies and eighties Nova Scotia owned more sailing vessels per head of population than any other country on the face of the earth, but that has gone due entirely, as already said, to steam superseding sail. While I do not often do so, on this occasion I support the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough because I think we should have marine schools at Halifax, Lunenburg, Canso, Sydney and Pictou. The total cost need not run into large figures, but these schools should be provided, where our young men would have the opportunity of attending them, and that without any undue expense. My hon. friend the "Admiral" has alluded to the fact that at present many of the commanders of the best liners on the Atlantic are Nova Scotians. Half the United States merchant fleet is officered by Nova Scotians, who in order to be able to serve on those ships have had to sacrifice their Canadian nationality. Our boats that are running to-day under government control to the West Indies are all manned and officered by Nova Scotians, all of whom got their first lessons in seamanship under sail. The total figure given by the minister for these schools does not amount to a bagatelle; let him double if and give these young men an opportunity to become efficient deep sea commanders.

subtopic: THE FIRTH-BREARLEY STAINLESS STEEL SYNDICATE LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is a bill to revive and extend the patents in respect of a certain invention commonly known as stainless steel. The reasons for which the legislation is asked are briefly as follows: The information I have before me sets out that the inventor, Harry Brearley, a British subject, residing in England, obtained a Canadian patent in 1915. In the normal course of events the patent expired at the end of August last. Prior to the date of expiration a petition was filed asking that it be extended for a period of six years, the reasons being as follows: This patent covers an alloy. Without going into the chemical properties of that alloy I may say that its outstanding property is the production of steel that is stainless in character, and is used largely in the manufacture of cutlery. The war being in progress the services of Mr. Brearley, the British inventor who was one of the leading engineers in the service of Thomas Firth and Sons, steel makers, were commandeered by the British government. The firms which developed the patent required to exert all their energies towards the construction of munitions until after the close of the war. So 
that for the period of the war and for some time following the inventor was unable to develop his invention.
The invention is set out briefly as follows: The production of the alloy, otherwise than for purposes of munitions, was from the first rendered practically impossible owing to the great scarcity of chromium, almost the whole of which was required for munitions, and the preoccupation of steel makers with war work and the necessity of utilizing the whole of the steel works output for government requirements. The British government for the time being prohibited entirely the manufacture of the alloy for purposes of manufacturing cutlery. At the time this prohibition was imposed the use of the alloy had not been developed for purposes other than cutlery and munitions, and therefore the prohibition of its use for the manufacture of cutlery practically amounted to a complete cessation of its manufacture for non-military purposes. So that so far as the inventor was concerned the years of the war were lost, and it was not until a couple of years afterwards that he could take steps to develop it. The patent is held by the parties named in the bill, namely The Firth-Brearley Stainless Steel Syndicate, Limited, which company is composed of the Firth of Thomas Firth and Sons and the original inventor, Brearley.
The principle of passing legislation to extend the ordinary life of a patent has been accepted on more than one occasion in this house. I took occasion to look up the precedents, and I have before me at least seven instances where similar action has been taken. Therefore I suggest that once the principle has been accepted we must face the question of merits. With this in mind I have indicated the merits of the present bill. If the house would be interested in having a list of precedents I shall state them briefly.
In 1930 the principle was acted upon in the case of an application by Stauntons Limited of the city of Toronto. In that instance the patent was extended from 1933 to 1938, a period of five years. In the case of the Canadian Cinch Anchoring Systems Limited of the city of Montreal, the patent was extended from 1930 to 1936, a period of six years. In the case of A. P. Frigon, of the city of Montreal, the patent was extended from 1922 to 1936, a period of fourteen years. In the case of Gold Medal Furniture Manufacturing Company of Toronto, the patent was extended from 1906 for a period of six years. In the case of the Facer Solid Steel Car Wheel Company Limited, of Perth, the

Supply-M arine
principle was acted upon and the extension obtained for a period of nine years. This bill asks for an extension of six years, being the time which it is estimated was lost.

Before the recess I listened with a great deal of pleasure to the plea made by hon. members from Nova Scotia for the establishment of three other schools of instruction in that province. I noted that the minister in his explanation stated that there were already two schools in that province, one at Yarmouth and the other at Halifax. I also noted that the number of students who attended these schools during the last year was two at Yarmouth and six ait Halifax, while the school at Quebec had an average of sixteen students during the season. If we are to judge by numbers, those figures might go to prove that the sailors of the province of Quebec take a stranger interest in the school of instruction than do the sailors in the maritime provinces.
In view of the admirable patience with which the minister has listened to the pleas that were made to him I venture to call his attention to the needs of the lower St. Lawrence, including the counties of Temiscouata, Rimouski and Matane. As the minister very well knows, sailors' families have been estab-tised in all the parishes of these counties for over a century, and the officers and men who man the fleets running from Montreal down to Matane come from these families. The minister knows how expensive it would be for the sons of these families to travel from points further down the river to the city of Quebec to take a course of instruction at the school there. He will recall that in the county of Rimouski at Father Point is situated the pilot station for the lower St. Lawrence, and there he has an officer of his department, an
Supply-M arine

ex-pilot, a very well educated man, who is extremely well qualified to take charge of one of these schools of instruction. I am asking the minister seriously to consider the establishment during the winter of a school of instruction at Father Point so that the sons of these families will have the opportunity of getting instruction. I can assure him that the expense connected with such a school would fee absolutely nil because the school itself could be located free of cost either through the municipal council or in one of the buildings belonging to the Department of Marine or the Department of Public Works. Secondly, the instructor for such a school could be chosen from among the present personnel of the Marine department at Father Point. Captain Lachance would be an admirable instructor for such a school. I have already spoken of his qualifications. He is paid his full salary during the summer but receives only part-time salary during the winter. If he were paid his full salary for the whole year I am sure that he would be very willing indeed to undertake this task.
I make this appeal to the minister because like many of my colleagues in the house I have received numerous applications and de1-mands for such a school, and we could do no more than refer them to the Department of Marine, where they have been told that the only school that exists in the province of Quebec was in the city of Quebec. The great majority of those who would like to take instruction in such a school could not possibly afford to pay their travelling expenses to Quebec and pay for their board there. It must be borne in mind that no allowance is made to the students attending these schools. They do not receive their railway fare or anything of the kind, but have to pay all their own expenses. In these times of stress it will be realized that it is not simply inconvenient but practically impossible for these young students to attend these schools, and therefore I hope the minister will give us people of the lower St. Lawrence the same- shall I say?-favourable consideration that he has promised those of the maritime provinces.

On behalf of the fishermen and mariners of northern British Columbia I wish to thank the Minister of Marine for establishing one of these schools of instruction at Prince Rupert. I have received many letters of appreciation of the fine service which the school at Prince Rupert is rendering, and I am therefore sorry to see that this vote is being reduced. These Canadian men make their living from the sea and this school is a great thing for them.

Instead of decreasing the vote I think it should be increased, but I thank the minister on their behalf for establishing the school. The young men of Canada who make their living from the sea should receive every encouragement.
