Will the minister and the hon. gentleman permit me to reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan)? The hon. gentleman mentioned the coloured ratings on the West Indies ships. I hold in my hand a file dealing with the matter, so the hon. gentleman will understand that this is rather an old question. I shall read some paragraphs from a letter of Mr. Allan, general manager of the Canadian National Steamships, to show the position they take in the matter:
What these men actually want is to replace the West Indians on the vagabond cruise boats, to which, of course, we have no objection whatever provided (1) they will accept the same wages a.nd (2) we can be assured that the service will not deteriorate thereby. It is most unsatisfactory to have half the crew engaged in Canada and the other half in the West Indies, as this means opening two sets of articles and causes confusion.
I have promised a delegation of these men to give the matter some very serious thought, and if it is possible to work out an arrangement whereby they can be employed I will do so, but we will be in the unfortunate position that in the event of these men leaving in the summer time when these vessels proceed to Montreal, we may have to go short of ratings or depend upon picking up further men when the vessels return to Halifax.
The three eastern passenger vessels, namely the Lady Nelson, Lady Drake and Lady Hawkins, now all carry white ratings. The additional expense to the company in breakage, etc., is averaging just about $500 a trip notwithstanding the fact that the men are paid the same wages as were the West Indians; the service is also falling off and we are changing approximately 40 per cent of the men each voyage in an endeavour to establish a satisfactory service.
In explanation of the last paragraph I may say that the fact was that a good many Canadians, both white and coloured, objected to the fact that there were so many West Indians on these boats, and wished to get the positions. The white Canadians who were

asking for the positions-this is about a year ago-were mostly dining ear men who were not accustomed to working on ships. Also there are other points that have been put to me in this file, not by Mr. Allan, but by others, which make it a very complicated question which I prefer not to discuss here in the house, but shall be glad to discuss with my hon. friend on some private occasion, because it deals with matters that do not interest the house as a whole and that may be misunderstood. I should like to inquire from the minister whether this semi-dual control which has been tried now for over a year is in his opinion working out satisfactorily. With departmental officials looking after reception, and with the sending stations in the hands of the radio commission, it does seem as if the present system was bound to lead to trouble. I can say quite candidly that the departmental officials must find it mighty hard to give satisfaction. It is not the fault of the department, but is the result of the adoption of wave lengths which apparently conflict with some of the more powerful stations across the line. I am wondering just where we are going to land with this whole radio business in Canada, and whether we are always going to be subject to interference in reception on the part of our neighbours to the south. There are times in Ottawa when it is utterly impossible to get anything like decent reception. It is not the fault of the receiving set or of the officials of the department who are trying to remove interference; it is because our sending stations clash with the much more powerful stations to the south. It does sefem to me that something might be done by changing the wave lengths. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Construction, maintenance and supervision of aids to navigation, including salaries and allowances to lightkeepers, $1,674,000.

This includes salaries and
allowances to lightkeepers. Three years ago, when this government decided to reduce the salaries of all public employees by ten per cent I protested vigorously, not only as that action affected lightkeepers but as it affected every other class of citizen, including judges. At that time I expressed the opinion that it was very poor policy and would not mean anything; I said it would not enable the government to balance the budget. My prophecy has been fulfilled; the money retained from civil servants-lightkeepers, charwomen, elevator men and others-

And members of
parliament.

Yes, and members of parliament; I was opposed to that too, and I was the only one that said so. I said at the time that it was not good policy and would not mean anything, because the very fact that this government gave the lead in the reduction of salaries induced employers of labour all over the country to do the same. It gave them the chance to reduce the salaries of their employees, and to-day we have before the committee which is sitting in this house investigating conditions in different manufacturing plants and other businesses in this country, an example of what this policy has meant. It shows conclusively to my mind that this government is partly to blame for conditions in the sweatshops where poor labouring people work practically for nothing. Now, here are lightkeepers in this country, situated away on rocky promontories and islands scattered throughout the Atlantic, the gulf of St. Lawrence, the great lakes and the Pacific, without facilities for educating their children. Half the time, especially in winter, these children cannot go to school. It is not fair that men in this class, filling responsible positions, most of them receiving very small salaries, should have had their remuneration

Supply-M arine
cut by ten per cent. Before this item carries I should like to have a statement from the minister so far as he himself at any rate is concerned. We have just passed another item of S3,750,000, representing an increase over the previous year of 81,459,650, and if the minister had sufficient influence with his colleagues to get that increase of a million and a half-I congratulate him on that achievement; I am not objecting to it-then I think he ought to bring his influence to bear in behalf of these employees in his department. He is bighearted and he has a good open countenance, and I suggest to him that he should approach his colleagues at the first opportunity and urge them not to renew the act which has been in force for the last two years, whereby the salary of the Minister of Justice, and my indemnity as well, have been reduced by ten per cent. I plead on behalf of the lightkeepers, because I think the minister should be the first man to take the initial step to urge upon the Prime Minister and other members of the cabinet the restoration to these employees of their full remuneration. If there are any people who are entitled to full remuneration it is these particular employees. Most of them get very small salaries and I would like the minister to ask his colleagues that these salaries be reinstated at one hundred per cent instead of ninety per cent. Before this item passes I should like some assurance from the minister on that point.

I would call attention to the fact that the salaries as included in the item do not provide for the ten per cent deduction because there is no footnote at the bottom as there is in the case of other items. Therefore the salaries are voted in toto.
The deduction is there just the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I have listened with keen interest to my hon. friend's remarks. I have the greatest sympathy for the lighthouse keepers, and I fully agree with him when he says that these civil servants have a hard job to perform and should be protected as much as possible. But I would like to remind him that the ten per cent deduction was not made for pleasure; it was made because we thought that for the purposes of economy civil servants should contribute as other citizens are doing towards the reduction of our yearly expenditures. But I can tell my hon. friend that the promise made by the government two years ago and again last year will be kept and the moment business
improved sufficiently the ten per cent reduction will disappear. I cannot make any promise for this year; it may be this year, but as soon as possible we will do away with the reduction.

I am very glad to hear the words of the minister. He said that this was done for the sake of economy; that it was not a pleasure to do it. As I said the first year this matter was brought up in the house, it was false economy. I said that it was not in the best interests of the country that the deduction should be made, because the government took 88,000,000 out of the pockets of its employees and therefore that money could not be spent in the country. Then I said that it had an influence with every employer of labour in Canada who wanted an excuse to reduce the salaries of his employees or labourers. In this way the deduction had a double-barrelled effect. It is all very well for the minister to say very seriously-and I know he is sincere-that he will endeavour to do what he can. What I am saying to the minister and what I said before is this: before he got an increase of about $1,500,000 making a total of $3,750,000 for dredging the St. Lawrence, the first thing he should have done was to have the salaries of the lighthouse keepers put back to the one hundred per cent. The hon. member for Rimouski said that the item did not provide for a ten per cent deduction.
There is no footnote.

I know that, but I am afraid this item of $1,434,000 is made up on a basis of ninety per cent of salaries instead of one hundred per cent. Will the minister kindly tell me or the hon. member for Rimouski who is correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: So far as salaries are concerned, this includes only ninety per cent.

Last year when this item was up I brought to the attention of the minister a very unfair situation in connection with lighthouse keepers' salaries, to which the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough has referred. There are cases where the department provides living quarters for the lighthouse keeper, and in making the deduction of the ten per cent, not only does it deduct ten per cent from the salary which the lighthouse keeper receives, but it also estimates the value of the living quarters to the man who occupies them and deducts from his wages ten per cent of that estimated value, which is money that he really never gets.
Supply-M mine
That is not a statement of fact.

It is.
Mr. MACiDOUGAiLL: No, it is not.

Well, we will allow the minister to decide. To my mind such a procedure is unfair. It is hard enough for a man to have ten per cent deducted from money he actually receives, but to have an additional deduction made in respect of the estimated value of his living quarters is really treating the lighthouse keeper unfairly. I know this to be a positive fact. The hon. member for Inverness thinks it is not correct, but men in my constituency have come and showed me their accounts and said: We are subject to a reduction of not only ten per cent, but fifteen or twenty per cent. I wrote to the department and that was the explanation, that in addition to the deduction of ten per cent from the regular monthly payments received by them from the department, they were also charged ten per cent on the estimated value of their living quarters. That is extremely unfair and the1 minister should remedy it.

I am not prepared to admit that it is unfair, because the rent paid by a civil servant is paid out of his salary. There is nothing extraordinary in that. If something is allowed for the residence of a lightkeeper, it is small, as a rule about $200, but it is supposed to be part of his remuneration just like that of any other employee who gets so much salary and pays his own rent. There is no difference at all.
speakername: Mr.   D U R AN LEA II@

speechtext:
The minister imagines he has an argument there, but many of the lighthouse keepers are compelled to live in those residences. They have homes of their own a few miles away in which they would much rather live, but they are forced to live in the lighthouse in order to perform their duties and in many cases they are obliged to keep up a home some miles away in order, as the hon. member for Antigonish-Guys-borough has said, that their children may be able to go to school, because in some cases the lighthouse keepers are in places where it is impossible for the children to go to school if they live in the lighthouses. Therefore these living quarters are of no benefit to them; they are forced to contribute ten per cent of the value that the department may put upon those living quarters. I contend that this is absolutely unfair.
Mr. MAODOUGAiLL: Has there been any change in the regulations regarding lighthouse

keepers since my hon. friend supported the former Liberal government in 1922?

The answer to that question is that a Liberal government never deducted ten per cent from any man's salary whether he was a lighthouse keeper or anybody else. This is the first government that has attempted to do that, so that the effect was not visible before.

I remember very well the time I was arguing with the hon. member for Inverness about minimum wage laws and I was telling him that they should have minimum wage laws in Nova Scotia, the hon. member said that they were superfluous. At that time we were fighting for all the labourers throughout the country from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and my hon. friend was not defending the case of the miners who received such small wages in Inverness and other parts of Cape Breton.
I am not answering any imbecility.

How many pilots have we in Canada? Is there a fixed yearly remuneration, or is it based on what they collect in each port? I have had many complaints; some pilots, I understand, get up to $20,000 and others are not getting anything, although they are all supposed to perform the same service-take charge of boats that come into certain harbours.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The pilotage districts are: Quebec, with fifty-three pilots; Montreal, with sixty-two; Halifax, twenty-three; Saint John, eleven; Sidney, fifteen; British Columbia, thirty-two, and Churchill, two. They are not all paid on the same basis; some are paid on the tonnage of the vessel and others on the draft of the vessel. It depends on the arrangements made.

Supply-Marine-Pilotage

How much does
the highest receive, and how much the lowest, and where is the one that receives the highest and the one that receives the lowest?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
There is no salary;
the pilot gets what he earns. I know that at Montreal and Quebec there is a pool into which the pilots bring their earnings. They pay the expenses and their superannuation contributions and the rest is divided among themselves. That is what is done as a rule in these pilots' associations.
How much would a pilot in Montreal get after all deductions, and a pilot in Vancouver?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I cannot say exactly
what they get. I know that the pilot in Montreal having the highest gross earnings during last season got $7,000. Rut they have to pay their travelling expenses out of that and their superannuation. I think the average net earnings run about $3,500 to $4,000. But I would remind my hon. friend that these pilots do not start earning money until they are over thirty. Apprentice pilots earn practically nothing for seven or ten years. I know assistant pilots who have been in the service for ten years now, and they cannot be admitted as pilots; according to the regulations the number of pilots cannot be increased, as each pilot is supposed to make so many voyages during the navigation season. So long as that average is not exceeded an assistant pilot is not admitted as a pilot. Sometimes a pilot starts earning his living at thirty-five years of age, and then does not work for a great many years as his eyesight must be first class; the moment he cannot pass the eyesight examination he has to retire.
What do they live on before they start earning?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Well, they get a few dollars. They work as mate or as assistant, and sometimes the assistant gets a little reward from the owner of the ship.

I have some
figures from Vancouver, and it seems to me ridiculous that men should get such pay. That is why I am asking for these particulars so that I can see whether these figures are right or wrong. I would like the minister also to let us know what a chief pilot for British Columbia or the Pacific coast gets in gross earnings. I have some figures from the statistical department; they must be reasonably accurate, but I would like to have them verified by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I am not in a position to give the information at the present time, but if my hon. friend has a particular case in mind I shall be pleased to take it up.
If the minister has the information as to pilots in Montreal he surely can give it in regard to pilots in Vancouver.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Well, I have the
information as to Montreal, but unfortunately I have not got it for Vancouver. I can write to my hon. friend and give him the full information if he desires.
I wish the minister would do that.
'Could the minister tell the committee what arrangement the pilots work under in British Columbia? I understand they have some cooperative arrangement, but I am not familiar with the details.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I suppose my hon.
friend knows that the pilotage is not compulsory on the British Columbia coast. Some companies have their own pilots; in fact I believe the Canadian Pacific has. I suppose those men are salaried. *
I was not asking the minister for details as to remuneration, but was directing my remarks to regulations controlling pilots in British Columbia.

I should be glad to
send the hon. member a copy of the British Columbia pilot regulations.

I believe thirty-two is
the fixed number of pilots. At the same time I should like to know what competition there is when someone wishes to become a pilot.

I shall supply the
necessary information.
At this very moment who is the pilot of the ship of state in this House of Commons?

member knows that most of the money voted, previously was loaned to the pilots' association. At this time they are collecting faster, and do not need so great a loan.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The sum of $23,039 represents an amount a little greater than that which was actually spent in 1933-34. We expect to be able to carry on with the same amount. Last year we did not spend everything that was voted.
Would the minister give the list of publications?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I should be happy to supply the hon. member with a list; it is a very long one.
Probably it could be placed on Hansard.

speechtext: Perhaps I did not understand the hon. member's question. This vote is not for the actual publishing or printing of the publications, but provides for payment to the personnel or staff which sends them out. I believe it includes also the cost of envelopes.
How many are engaged in this work of sending out publications?

speechtext: In the neighbourhood of twenty-nine or thirty, permanent or regular. Then there is a small temporary staff which from time to time is required to keep up with the work.

May I ask the minister how a farmer is to know what publications are available? Is a list supplied to him? Must he write in, or how is he to obtain the information? Further, to whom is the information sent without application?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: There is a list of publications together with supplementary lists of new publications. Any farmer writing to the department will have sent to him any special publication he wishes, and included in each publication there will be a list of all publications which, if he wishes he may send for.
Why is there a decrease in the vote for these publications, if they are all so important?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I have explained
that there is not an actual decrease. We did not use all the money voted last year, so we are asking for a smaller amount this year.
Did I understand the minister to say his department employed twenty-nine or thirty persons to send out the publications of his department?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That is correct.
What is the average salary paid to these employees?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I have not that information before me, but shall be glad to send it to the hon. member.
How many publications per month do they send?

Do I understand that these publications are sent only on request, or does the department send them to public libraries, universities, and so on?

Supply-Agriculture-Publications

speechtext: There are mailing lists. If a farmer for instance, sends in and asks for a publication his name would be added to the list. We also have lists of libraries, agricultural societies and various associations. We keep those mailing lists and send out the new publications.
Is the circulation nationwide?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes.
In what parts of Canada is the circulation greatest? I should like to know where this special information is going.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I think the answer would be where there is the greatest number of farmers.

If my information is correct the number of publications has been curtailed in* the last few years. As a member of parliament I used to get several more publications from the department than I do now, and these publications were in most cases of great service to the farmers and settlers in our section. I should like to ask if that is the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I am quite certain that no publications that are available will be refused on request of any person. There is no curtailment in the sending out of publications published for general distribution.

I think members of parliament, senators and officials should be placed on the mailing list, because I have found these publications of great service. A member of parliament receiving them can distribute them to the farmers in his riding who are likely to benefit from the information. I think it should be possible for the minister to do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We shall be glad to include the members of parliament who are not already included on the mailing list.
Provided they can read them.

I understood the minister to say that this item of $22,000 is not to pay for the publications but for the expense of sending them out. It does not cover the salaries of those engaged in preparing the publications?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That is correct.
It is just to pay the expense of wrapping and sending them out?

speechtext: Yes, operation costs together with supplies.

I should like to draw the attention of the minister to something that very often happens in my district. We have students taking short courses, and in many instances when we ask for a certain number of publications for distribution to these students our requests have been turned down. I think these publications should be distributed to the students in these short courses. In other instances, a professor in an agricultural institution will ask for a certain number of publications, and in some instances in the past, although not quite recently, his request has been refused. The department will reply suggesting that the students themselves write in for the publication. Now it is sometimes a troublesome thing for a farmer to get a pen and sit down and write a letter, and very often he does not know to whom to send it. I think it would be very much better if the department would comply with these requests for various publications from public bodies and organizers of short courses.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: There is no reason whatever why that should not be done if the publication is still available. I believe that in the past, including the more recent past, difficulty has arisen through members of parliament as well as people outside asking for large bulk lots. It was felt that there was perhaps a good deal of wastage in that connection. However, I agree with my hon. friend that there is no place where better use could be made of these publications than in connection with university work and short courses.

I asked the minister
where the circulation of these publications was the greatest. The minister answered, among the farmers. Perhaps he misunderstood my question. I wanted to know in what part of Canada, in what economic area, there is the largest circulation of these publications.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
My answer was
not " among the farmers " but where the farmers are the most numerous, particularly where there is specialization in poultry, fruit and so forth. More publications are sent there as a rule.
How often is the mailing list revised?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
There is a list of
publications at the beginning of each year, and as new publications come out a supplementary list is sent along to those receiving

the original list. At the end of each year an attempt is made to combine as far as possible the new publications and the old in a revised list.

He considered that it was very important that the information should be compiled from the various sources and sent out to the farmer on the ground that through the written word more farmers could be reached than in any other way, and with less expense. speechtext:
As a matter of
fact the demand for the publications is increasing. Although the vote has been decreased the number of publications sent out is increasing to a considerable extent. In 1922-23 the number of publications sent out, annual reports, bulletins, pamphlets, circulars, orders and regulations, was 776,906; in 1932-33, over

1932-	33. The mailing lists have also been added to considerably, and that is a very good indication that there is a greater demand for the publications. That demand has been met to a greater extent. The number of names on the mailing lists, special and general lists, in 1922-23 was 308,595 and in 1932-33, 550,907. Requests for publications from individuals are not as great at the present time as in 1927-28, but the number of the more important publications sent out has increased.
'Mr. DUPUIS:	May I suggest to the
minister that he did not answer the question asked by the ex-Minister of Agriculture. I understood his question to 'be why there was a decrease in this vote from $28,000 in 1933-34 to $23,000 in 1934-35, and the minister in his reply referred to 1932-33, and not to
1933-	34.

speechtext:
That might have
been caused by larger amounts being voted than were actually used. As far as I am aware, there has always been a sufficient amount voted to meet the requests of the public for publications.

"Might have been"
is no answer. In 1932-33 the vote was only $7,500; if that amount was sufficient, why should it be raised to $23,000? There must be some other reason.

speechtext: When the vote was in the neighbourhood of $7,000 it was found that that was not sufficient. Certain publications could not be sent out when requested and they had to be sent out by the various branches of the department.

Perhaps this would be as good a time as any to remark on the general tendency to decrease practically every vote for agriculture. This year there has been a decrease in every vote but two, and every year we see these votes decreasing and decreasing. This would seem to be a time when agriculture should receive an increase in assistance rather than suffer a decrease. If any of us were sick he would want more care at that time than when he was well. Now agriculture is decidedly sick not only in Canada but the world over; yet we have withdrawn aid from a sick institution at a time when we should be nursing it. That is the complaint I have to make with regard to these estimates. There is a progressive reduction year after year, and if this keeps up, and if my good friend should have the opportunity of presiding over the department another four years, I am afraid the estimates and his department will have disappeared altogether by that time unless something is done to stop the downward tendency. I would convey my remarks as much to the hon. gentleman's colleagues as to himself. Since the revenues are supposed to be improving, and I think they are, I would bespeak a reasonable amount of the increase which is accruing from month to month to be devoted to the Department of Agriculture. I do not know what department will be instrumental in getting Canada back on her feet more than agriculture. That industry represents more people than any other in the dominion. I do not blame the Minister of Finance so much either, because after all it is the Prime Minister who has to say definitely what each department shall receive. It looks to me that the trouble lies between the minister and the Prime Minister so far as this regrettable continuous reduction in estimates for agriculture is concerned. This year it is lower than ever by three-quarters of a million; it is down to what it was about ten years ago, six and a half millions.
I am really getting anxious, wondering where this downward tendency will stop, and I hold the ministry as a whole rather than the Minister of Agriculture responsible for this absolute neglect of the major occupation of the people of Canada. I spoke of this last year and I will not speak harshly about it any more. I merely direct the attention of the ministry to this tendency towards a seeming neglect of the major occupation of the Canadian people. Why it should be I do not know. Evidently the relative importance of

this industry has not yet been seized by the government, or it would have been given visibility to, in these estimates, by an upward rather than a downward tendency. I can only express my regret at it as I have done on former occasions, and I hope that the minister and his colleagues present will do something to stop this tendency. I am sure the minister's estimates go to the treasury board much larger than this; I feel confident that they do.
I know that the heads of branches must ask for more than they get, and the matter must come in that shape before the ministry and the subcommittee of government called the treasury board. So that the whole government is to be held responsible for this, and I do not think the excuse of low revenues is sufficient to justify the decrease. Canada can never come back until agriculture shows a tendency to come back, and consequently the props should be strengthened under this department instead of being jolted from under it.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
It is only natural
that the hon. member (Mr. Motherwell) should be struck in this way with the reduction of estimates. The test I keep before me each year when the estimates are submitted and agreed to-and so far I have had no difficulty in having the request met-is this that the services in each branch will not be in any way impaired. A large number of reductions have been made possible, for instance by reorganization. I might refer to the live stock branch, but I do not wish to open up this matter here because I should prefer to have the items dealt with item by item. I can assure hon. members however that there has been no depreciation in the services given in each of these votes. In the majority of the votes there has been improved service as a result of reorganization within the particular branch, combining the heads of services, so that it is more flexible, uniting them in a common effort, than had been the case in various divisions before. Perhaps we have given the matter more attention because of the period of economic depression through which we have been passing; it has been necessary for us to endeavour, as we might not have done had it not been for the present financial condition, to make every effort to reorganize in order to save money. But we have always kept before us the one yardstick, namely, that there should be no depreciation in any service rendered agriculture in the various branches. And in most branches the services have been actually strengthened.

There is something in that, but I am afraid that reason does not quite satisfy my hon. friend himself. He better than anyone else must know that some of the activities of the various branches have been reduced, the staff being reduced, pos-s;bly owing to reorganization. However, we will not discuss this particular item, which is not so conspicuous as some others. In the Health of Animals branch, for example, the activities can hardly be as general and widespread in the establishment of restricted areas for instance, as in the past. However, we will leave that vote until we come to it. I think my hon. friend knows better than anyone else that he has been jewing the votes down year by year, pinching off here and pinching off there, until so to speak the work has its eyes sticking out, wondering what is going to happen next.
I know you cannot make a substantial reduction in each of these estimates without affecting the service. You can lop off a few salaries, dismiss a few employees, getting rid of them by reorganization, and while that may effect a small saving I do not know but even that will have an injurious effect on the service. But generally, in the main work of the field men throughout Canada, whether it is one branch or the other, I am afraid you cannot take off four millions in three years without substantially reducing services, some here and some there, all making a considerable aggregate. If it can be done this way, how would it do to make the vote for agriculture a little lower still and save that much more money? I am afraid my hon. friend has come long ago to the point where no further reductions can be made without sacrificing the work to a considerable extent. There is something, possibly, in what th-e minister says in regard to reorganization, and perhaps some slight saving has been effected there. But to cut tlhe aggregate vote nearly in two and at the same time to maintain the services is a suggestion which I am not quite prepared to accept at its full face value; not that I doubt my hon. friend's statement, but I do not think it can be done by anyone. Nor do I think my hon. friend believes it can be done, if he will analyse the work and compare it with what was in vogue a few years ago. However, maybe we have now come to the bottom of these ruthless cuts. Now that we are looking forward to the salary cuts being restored-the newspapers say there are prospects of it-maybe we have got to the bottom of these successive declines in agricultural appropriations. In other words maybe we

have touched bottom in the matter of reduction in the agricultural estimates and another year will see a revival, an upward tendency. If that happens, I shall be the first to congratulate ourselves, the government and the minister.

I put that on record because I think we cannot too often emphasize the necessity of maintaining high quality production, nor do I think we can too often emphasize the necessity of grading our farm products. Since the principle of cream grading has been adopted in Manitoba and has been consistently adhered to, the work being done in conjunction with the very effective dairy commissioner in that province, the result has been as I have indicated. Nobody will contend that commercial butter is equal to that which appears at these exhibitions, but the fact that this record has been made is to my mind a strong argument for the maintenance of the grading of our cream and of all our other dairy products.

Perhaps just in this connection I might mention poultry. If there is one thing that has been an outstanding success in the west, it is the poultry pools where under government auspices or through the initiative of the government some years ago an expert poultry man was sent out. When we began to ship poultry through those pools some of the stuff that was brought in was so poor the people had to take it home again; it would not be accepted. But the people who brought that stuff in were able to see what good, properly dressed poultry really was, and the consequence has been that the whole standard of dressed poultry has been raised, due undoubtedly to. the fact that this system of grading has been adopted. People have been able to see what good poultry is.
Speaking again on the grading of cream,
I am not certain of this figure, but I heard it asserted that sixty per cent of the cream delivered to the creameries in Manitoba last year was table cream. People thought at "first cream was simply cream, but they very soon learned that when cream was paid for by the grade, it paid them to take good care of their cream. I do not want to cast reflections upon other provinces, but some objection has pretty persistently come from Quebec. I can say this, that from my knowledge of Quebec there is no other country in the world better suited to the production of high quality butter than the eastern townships of Quebec and the Laurentian mountains across the Ottawa river. They have splendid pasture and the very best of running water, and there is no reason why a high quality of butter could not be produced. I know they tell us that it pays them better to produce cream and I know also very large quantities of milk from Quebec go into Montreal as liquid milk; but still I maintain that if the producers adopt and consistently adhere to the principle of the grading of cream as we have done in Manitoba, all the provinces will be able to come somewhere near the level that has been attained in my province.
Does the hon. member give the government any credit for that?
Why, certainly.

This was going on long
before the present government came into power. I might say that as far back as 1924 the records were as high. I am willing to give the Minister of Agriculture every credit for consistently adhering to the system of grading farm products, and I am only sorry he has not had much support from eastern Canada up to date.
